newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir poll victory may bring autonomy closer.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir poll victory may bring autonomy closer.

text.p: The largest pro-India party in Jammu and Kashmir state won an absolute majority in the first state assembly elections since the outbreak of a separatist rebellion in 1990, results showed on Wednesday.
The vote is seen appeasing some of fractious Kashmir's long-standing demands for greater autonomy.
The moderate National Conference party, led by former chief minister Farooq Abdullah, won 52 seats in the state's 87-member assembly, election officials said.

"The results are very close to our expectations," said Saifuddin Soz, the National Conference spokesman. "We are particularly hopeful that our plank on enlargement of autonomy has been accepted by the people."

India's constitution originally gave Kashmiris nominal control over most affairs, but New Delhi has gradually eroded these powers since 1952. The National Conference wants to recapture some of them to help subdue the separatist movement.
Abdullah was chief minister when the insurgency erupted in early 1990.

The National Conference had a commanding lead over its rivals. Trailing far behind were the Congress party and the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), each with seven seats. Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's Janata Dal party had five.
Congress spokesman Gulam Rasool Kar said his party admitted defeat. "We will provide full support to the National Conference in running the government," he added.
"Of course Dr Abdullah will be the next chief minister," said Mohammed Syed Akhoon, a jubilant leader of the National Conference party.
"He is the only one who can give honourable status to Kashmiris."

Abdullah, who escaped two grenade attacks in the month-long elections, has called for a greater degree of autonomy for the Himalayan state, torn by the six-year separatist revolt, but has promised to continue a crackdown on militants.

India accuses Pakistan, which rules over one third of the disputed Kashmir region, of funding and arming separatist guerrillas. Islamabad denies the charge, saying it extends them only moral and political support.

Abdullah's party refused to participate in parliamentary elections held earlier this year, saying that the Congress government of then prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao was not committed to meeting his party's autonomy demands.
But after Deve Gowda assumed power in June, his centre-left United Front coalition pledged "maximum autonomy" to mostly Hindu India's only Moslem majority state.
The National Conference decided to participate in last month's local assembly polls anticipating an autonomy package.

Under the Indian constitution, the state has nominal control over its affairs except in defence, foreign affairs and communications. New Delhi has taken control of these, many Kashmiris say, and look to Abdullah to reclaim them.

However, the BJP has promised to oppose any move in the federal parliament to grant special status to Jammu and Kashmir, made up of the mostly Moslem Kashmir valley, the Hindu majority Jammu region and Buddhist Ladakh.
